props.title: Rats
props.initialSlug: Vicious rats terrorize a small town's residents

sections.content: Rats (2003) dives deep into New York City's eternal battle with its most notorious pest, delivering a fascinating documentary that's equal parts horror show and urban sociology. Director Morgan Spurlock (who would later make Super Size Me (2004)) crafts an unflinching look at how rats have adapted to thrive alongside humans. The film shares DNA with other urban wildlife documentaries like Dark Days (2000) about NYC's subway tunnel dwellers, but adds a visceral element that makes viewers squirm.

sections.content: The film taps into our primal fears while examining humanity's complex relationship with vermin. Like Night of the Living Dead (1968) used zombies to explore social issues, Rats uses its subject to illuminate class divisions, urban decay, and public health challenges. The documentary's unflinching camera work recalls the shocking directness of Mondo Cane (1962), while its exploration of urban ecosystems shares themes with Koyaanisqatsi (1982).

What elevates Rats beyond mere shock value is its examination of different cultural attitudes toward these creatures. From New York exterminators to Indian temples where rats are revered, the film challenges Western perspectives. This anthropological approach mirrors other documentaries like Gates of Heaven (1978) and Vernon, Florida (1981) that find profound insights in seemingly mundane subjects. SUBHEAD: Urban Wildlife & Human Coexistence

sections.content: The film's exploration of urban ecology connects to other documentaries examining how wildlife adapts to human environments. The Biggest Little Farm (2018) shows how even small changes in human behavior can dramatically impact local ecosystems. Cane Toads: An Unnatural History (1988) similarly examines how introduced species can overwhelm urban environments, while Planet Earth II (2016) dedicates an entire episode to how animals survive in cities.
